newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Main events in road to Swiss Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Main events in road to Swiss Holocaust fund.

text.p: Chronology of main events leading to the first board meeting of the Swiss Holocaust Memorial Fund on Monday:
1995 - Foreign and domestic criticism grows regarding Swiss banks' handling of dormant accounts of Holocaust victims and the country's purchases of looted gold from Nazi Germany during World War Two.
March 27, 1995 - Member of Parliament Verena Grendelmeier launches initiative with goal of government decree on tracking down and returning dormant wealth.

September 8, 1995 - Swiss Bankers Association issues new guidelines on how members should handle dormant accounts, agrees to set up ombudsman who will coordinate requests for information from potential claimants.
February 7, 1996 - Ombudsman's survey finds around 38.7 million Swiss francs in unclaimed wealth in bank accounts opened before 1945. World Jewish Congress estimates the amount is much higher.
April 23 - U.S. Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato starts hearings on Swiss banks' handling of dormant accounts.

May 2 - Swiss bankers and Jewish groups agree to create independent panel to search for any unclaimed wealth at Swiss banks. Former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker named head of the panel in August.
September 30, 1996 - Lower house of parliament approves federal decree calling for probe of Swiss role as financial centre during World War Two.

October 3 - Auschwitz survivor Gizella Weisshaus files class-action suit in New York against two big Swiss banks asking $20 billion for Nazi victims. Five other survivors file a separate suit against Swiss banks on October 23.

October 16 - Senator D'Amato cites U.S. archival material to allege Swiss used dormant wealth of Polish Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by Warsaw's post-war communist regime under 1949 treaty.
October 23 - Swiss foreign ministry asks two historians to probe D'Amato's allegations, creates task force to coordinate Swiss response to rising tide of accusations.

November 12 - After one-year search, banks' ombudsman says he has matched 1.6 million francs in dormant wealth to 11 rightful owners, but found only 11,000 francs owned by people persecuted by the Nazis.
November 18 - British MPs Greville Janner and Sir David Hunt call in Berne for quick creation of a fund to compensate recognised victims of the Nazis.
November 27 - Some Holocaust survivors call for boycott of Swiss banks in effort to prompt gesture to Hitler's victims.

December 11 - Task force chief Thomas Borer tells U.S. House of Representatives Banking Committee that Switzerland will quickly compile report on its wartime role; World Jewish Congress (WJC) President Edgar Bronfman and D'Amato seek financial gesture from Switzerland as a sign of good will.

December 13 - Parliament gives final approval to decree on sweeping historical probe of wartime era; Swiss National Bank says it has earned around 20 million francs through wartime gold transactions with Nazis.
December 19 - Government names nine-member international panel of historians to probe wartime era.

December 31 - Economics Minister and outgoing President Jean-Pascal Delamuraz likens Jewish calls for restitution to "extortion and blackmail" in newspaper interview, touching off protests and renewed threats of a boycott call.

January 7, 1997 - Swiss government calls for immediate talks with banks and Jewish groups on using dormant accounts to create Holocaust memorial fund, leaves open door for adding public money as a gesture of good will.

January 14 - Private security guard at Union Bank of Switzerland reveals he removed old documents bound for shredder at the bank and turned them over the Swiss Jewish leaders; UBS calls intended shredding a "regrettable mistake".
January 15 - Delamuraz apologises for blackmail remark.
January 22 - Credit Suisse Chairman Rainer Gut proposes that government, Swiss National Bank and private banks and insurers create humanitarian fund for Nazi victims and their relatives.
January 23 - Government welcomes Gut's call and says it will discuss creating fund with banks; officials agree in principle to proceed during talks with business executives.
January 26 - Newspaper publishes leaked document in which Swiss ambassador to Washington calls for "waging war" against Jewish groups and other critics, prompting envoy's resignation.
January 29 - New York city and state warn Switzerland they can make it tough for Swiss banks to do business there unless Swiss set up fund for Holocaust victims.
February 5 - Three biggest Swiss banks contribute 100 million Swiss francs to humanitarian fund for Holocaust victims; other businesses pledge to follow suit.
February 6 - Jewish leaders drop plans for Swiss bank boycott.
February 12 - Swiss government agrees to create immediately a memorial fund that taps contributions from banks and other businesses to aid Holocaust victims.
February 26 - Government gives final approval to fund after working out administrative details with Jewish groups

March 5 - Swiss President Arnold Koller proposes creating seven billion Swiss franc Swiss Solidarity Foundation that would use proceeds of official gold sales to finance humanitarian aid to victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights abuses.
April 16 - Swiss government appoints Rolf Bloch president of Holocaust memorial fund; names Josi Meier, Rene Bacher and Bernard Ziegler as Swiss members of board.
May 1 - Swiss government votes in Jewish representatives Elie Wiesel, Avraham Hirschson and Josef Burg to fund board.
May 9 - Nobel Peace Prize winner Wiesel declines to join the board.
May 28 - Swiss government elects WJC President Edgar Bronfman to replace Wiesel on board, names 18-member advisory council that will suggest which projects to support.
June 25 - Government backs 100 million Swiss franc contribution to fund from Swiss National Bank.
July 7 - Fund board holds first meeting.
